new.n: Plowville: the 1952 national plow matches (125,000 people)
new.pl: Farm fields by U.S. 14, about 1.5 miles east of Dodge Center
new.st: On 6 September 1952 Minnesota's first National Soil Conservation Districts' Field Day and Plow Matches drew 125,000 spectators to the farm fields here, and both presidential candidates, Dwight Eisenhower and Adlai Stevenson, spoke. The marker (H-59) says the site was donated in memory of J. L. Gossard.
new.t: One of the biggest one-day crowds in Minnesota history, spread over open farm fields: 1950s coins, tokens and campaign buttons. Private farmland: ask the owner.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots
pinev: Placed on U.S. 14 about 1.5 miles east of Dodge Center, where the marker stands; the fields used are not mapped, so good to about 800 m
Unconfirmed, one source

new.pl: About 1/4 mile south of the marker on Hwy 210, 1 mile west of Clitherall
new.v: Coins, buttons, household losses from the 1860s-80s
new.st: Settled in 1865 by Latter Day Saints, Old Clitherall broke up after the railroad built New Clitherall, and it has nearly disappeared (marker H-38).
new.t: Look for the house lots and the old road on a 1930s air photo first. Private land: ask first.

new.n: Itasca village and the 1849 Holmes & Beatty trading post
new.pl: 800 ft east of the Dayton Port roadside marker on U.S. 10, Anoka County
new.v: Trade goods, coins, buttons, oxcart parts
new.st: Holmes & Beatty set up a trading post here in 1849, 800 ft east of today's marker. A hotel followed in 1852, then the first post office in Anoka County, and the village became a Red River oxcart stop; in 1857 the carts brought $120,000 of furs, robes and meat. It was deserted by the early 1860s, though the post office lasted to 1879 and was the first mailing address of Oliver Kelley's National Grange. The marker says traces of the old oxcart trail can be seen a few feet west of it (H-98).
new.t: Look for the oxcart ruts west of the marker and the post site 800 ft east. Ask the owner; the highway right-of-way is off limits.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots
pinev: Placed 800 ft east of the Dayton Port stop on U.S. 10; good to about 300 m
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Troy Mill (1857-1900) on the Winona-Chatfield territorial road
new.v: Coins, tokens, harness and mill hardware
new.st: Joseph and Samuel Musser built a four-story mill here in 1857 on the old Winona-Chatfield territorial road. It was a meeting place and a refuge during Indian raids, ran until 1900 and was razed in 1943 (marker H-79).
new.t: Mill seat, millpond and the road stop around it. Private land: ask first.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

new.n: Samuel Pond's mission to the Shakopee Dakota (1847)
new.pl: East edge of Shakopee, by Hwy 101
new.v: Buttons, trade goods, coins, mission-house losses
new.st: Rev. Samuel W. Pond built a two-story frame mission here in 1847 for the Shakopee band of Dakota, with an eight-foot stockade around the house and a half-acre garden. The building was wrecked about 1907, and the marker (H-60) says its foundations remain. This is not the Gideon Pond house in Bloomington.
new.t: Look around the foundations and garden ground only with permission; mission grounds can hold burials, so stay off any graves.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

new.pl: Hwy 104 by Lake Johanna, south of Glenwood near Terrace, Pope County
new.st: A crude log fort on the 1863 frontier defense line, abandoned after a few months; neighbors hauled off the logs (marker H-93). The West Lake Johanna Cemetery is about 300 m from this pin and is look-only.
new.t: A short-lived fort: find the building pad on a 1930s air photo first. Ask the owner, and keep well clear of the cemetery.

new.st: Glencoe was laid out in 1855. In the winter of 1862-63 the town was heavily fortified and held by as many as four companies of troops (marker H-22).

new.n: Clifton: the first North Shore townsite (1855) and the French River copper shafts
new.pl: West of the French River mouth, St. Louis County
new.st: Clifton, platted in 1855 just west of the French River mouth, was the first townsite surveyed on the North Shore. The French River Mining Co. and North Shore Mining Co. sank exploratory shafts in 1864-66 but found no paying copper (marker H-74).
new.t: Old exploratory shafts are dangerous: look only near any opening. Private shore land: ask first.

fr-fountain-cave-st-paul.st: Marker H-84: known by 1811 and visited by Long (1817), Schoolcraft (1820) and Nicollet (1837). Pierre "Pig's Eye" Parrant's 1838 saloon, the first building in St. Paul, stood where the ravine met the river. Highway fill of the early 1960s buried the entrance, and there is no visible sign of the cave today.

fr-carver-s-cave-treaty-site-1767.st: Marker H-92: Jonathan Carver reached the cave ("Wakon-teebe") on 10 November 1766 and held council with 300 Dakota there in April 1767. Railroad building about 1869 partly destroyed it; the burial mounds above are look-only.

fr-little-rapids-fur-trading-posts-minne.st: Marker H-30 (U.S. 212, 1 mile west of Chaska): Jean B. Faribault traded here for the North West Co. by 1804, at the Little Rapids of the Minnesota 5 miles south of the marker.

ob-crow-wing-village.st: Marker H-40: a trading post stood opposite the Crow Wing River mouth from about 1826, a village grew around it, and in the 1860s the Red River trail crossed the Mississippi here before the town gradually disappeared. It is now Crow Wing State Park.

fr-bolles-flouring-mill-and-grindstone-q.st: Marker H-72 (Hwy 95 at the north edge of Afton): Lemuel Bolles built the first commercial flour mill in the Minnesota country about 1843 on Bolles Creek, a mile and a half upstream, and it ran until 1875.

hm-253.st: Marker H-78: Joseph R. Brown laid out the town of Dahcotah here in 1839 and built the Tamarack House as the St. Croix County courthouse, called the first capitol building in Minnesota. The townsite has vanished.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

vs-2073138.st: Marker H-3 (Hwy 108, 5 miles east of Ottertail): Leaf City was a trading post on the Red River trail by 1857, with a post office from 1857 to 1860, and was broken up by the 1862 war.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

fr-camp-pope-redwood-falls.st: Marker H-13: the 1863 troop concentration point about a mile north of the marker on Hwy 19; 3,300 men left on 16 June 1863 for the Missouri, and the camp was used again in 1864. The Camp Pope Burial Plot nearby is look-only.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

fr-kaposia-little-crow-s-village-sites-a.st: Markers H-10 and H-53: in June 1842 an Ojibwe war party attacked from the Battle Creek ravine. Kaposia village stood on the Mendota trail from 1839 to 1852 at the north edge of South St. Paul.

ab4-pokegama-mission.st: Markers H-43 and H-58: Rev. Frederick Ayer's mission and school for the Ojibwe stood on the east shore of Lake Pokegama, 3 miles west of the U.S. 61 marker 1 mile north of Pine City; it was founded in 1836 and abandoned in 1846 after the 1841 attack.

cem-640504.st: Marker M-9: two trenches east of the Brook Park fire monument hold 23 victims of the 1894 Hinckley fire; the Hinckley Memorial Cemetery holds 248 more in four trenches (M-17). These are graves: look only.

hm2-189.st: Marker H-46: one of three pentagonal green-timber blockhouses with 50-ft sides built at St. Joseph in August 1862; a second stood near St. Benedict's College.

t-rep-vermilion-1865.st: Marker H-66 (west edge of Tower): it displays an ore crusher "used in search for gold, one of the first pieces of mining equipment in the area", found under water in Trout Creek. Tower was the end of the Vermilion Trail, built from Duluth in 1865 for the gold rush prospectors.

ab4-chengwatana-village.st: Marker H-58 (Pine City): "A rich deposit of copper was discovered here and a $250,000 company was formed which sank some 150-foot shafts." The old copper mine site is not placed yet. Old shafts are dangerous: look only near any opening.

t-pan-oronoco.st: State marker H-106 at Oronoco State Wayside (U.S. 52 north of Oronoco): gold was found along the Zumbro in summer 1858, and several hundred men panned and sluiced until spring floods and the Panic of 1857 ended it. The marker was re-erected in 1967.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots

ab-fort-ripley.st: Marker H-103 (U.S. 371, 8 miles north of Camp Ripley Junction): built 1848-50 on the west bank opposite the marker, first called Fort Marcy and then Fort Gaines, and renamed Fort Ripley on 4 November 1850. Settlers sheltered here in 1862; it burned in 1877 and was abandoned in 1880, and a powder magazine ruin is the only stone left.
src: History Along the Highways: A Guide to Minnesota's Historic Markers and Sites (Minnesota Historical Society, 1967), your screenshots
